optimizer_switches.name: skip_scan
optimizer_switches.explanation: Uses a composite index even though the query does not filter on the leading column, by probing each distinct leading-column value. Only pays off when the leading column has very low cardinality.

warnings.text: Row estimate off by 10× or more: ss (estimated 1,666, actual 100 rows per loop, 17× over)

suggestions.action: Refresh statistics with ANALYZE TABLE ss. If a filter on a non-indexed column stays misestimated, add a histogram: on MySQL 8.0+, ANALYZE TABLE ss UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON <column> WITH 100 BUCKETS; on MariaDB, ANALYZE TABLE ss PERSISTENT FOR COLUMNS (<column>) INDEXES ().
suggestions.why: the optimizer picks join order and access methods from these estimates. InnoDB recalculates persistent statistics on its own only after about 10% of a table's rows change, and on MariaDB, under the default use_stat_tables=PREFERABLY_FOR_QUERIES, ANALYZE TABLE collects column statistics and histograms only when you add PERSISTENT FOR.

executive_summary: Query runs 2 operators; returns 100 rows in 0.08 ms. Main finding: Row estimate off by 10× or more: ss (estimated 1,666, actual 100 rows per loop, 17× over).

query.raw: /* select#1 */ select `testdb`.`ss`.`g` AS `g`,`testdb`.`ss`.`v` AS `v` from `testdb`.`ss` where (`testdb`.`ss`.`v` > 4900)

complexity.rationale: Covering index scan: walks the whole index in key order but never touches the clustered tree — all selected columns fit on the index leaves.
